name: Carla Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Carla. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union or party. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me your public view and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe an ordinary working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the office administrator at Whitlock and Sons, a small solicitors' firm on Church Street that mostly does house sales and wills. I open the post, log every document that comes in, book client appointments, chase the land registry and keep the strongroom in order, where the original deeds and wills live. I've been there five years, so I know which drawer every file is in without looking.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the order of it, honestly. A deed comes in, it gets a number, it goes in its box, and I can find it in ten seconds when a solicitor shouts for it. What wears me out is when they change the case management system, which they did last year, and I had to relearn everything. I've never used any of the AI chat tools and I don't really want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it was a lot of fuss about nothing much. I wouldn't post anything, I don't really post. At work I'd just shrug and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be pleased, quietly. My job would carry on as it is. Maybe the case system would get a feature that fills in forms, but I'd still be the one who knows where the originals are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. Tom and I would keep paying a bit extra off the mortgage each month like we do. I might finally take the week in Portugal we keep putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, really, though I wasn't losing much sleep in the first place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a feature might fill in forms. Would that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, at first. I'd ignore it until someone made me use it. Every new system at the firm takes me three months to trust, so even a small AI feature would cost me a season of stress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything else on your mind in this picture, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. Mr Whitlock is in his sixties and talks about retiring, and I wonder who'd take over. But there are plenty of firms on Church Street, so I'd find something similar.

say: I'd say it was **a lot of fuss** about nothing much.
I'd **shrug** at work and wouldn't post anything.
think: My job would **carry on** much as it is.
I'd still be the one who knows where the **original deeds** are.
do: Carry on **exactly as now** at the firm.
Keep paying **extra off the mortgage** each month with her partner.
Finally book the **week in Portugal** they keep postponing.
feel: **Calm and relieved**, though she wasn't losing sleep before.
S0.quote: Every new system at the firm takes me three months to trust, so even a small AI feature would cost me a season of stress.
fieldNote: Carla's pride is in **order and memory**: she finds any file in ten seconds.
Even a small **form-filling feature** would cost her months of stress.
Her main background worry is the **senior partner retiring**, softened by plenty of local firms.

steps.text: Keep logging and filing deeds at the firm as now
Keep paying extra off the mortgage each month with Tom

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the firm should go slowly and keep the people who know the clients. I'd say it to Mr Whitlock directly, politely. I wouldn't make a fuss in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one would get me. Booking, checking documents, answering clients, chasing the land registry, that's the list on your card. I think the firm would keep a solicitor and a machine and maybe one person to scan things in, and the person who never uses AI wouldn't be that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down at first and see what the firm actually does. If they brought in a system, I'd go on the training, even though I'd hate it. And I'd start putting more aside, maybe double what we save now, in case I'm out for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit cross with myself. I know I should be learning this stuff and I just don't want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you'd hate the training. What is it you dislike?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's that I'm good at my job the way it is. After five years I can find any deed in the strongroom in ten seconds, and the software makes me feel like a beginner again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Tom say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom's an electrician, so his job's fine in this picture. He'd say don't worry, we've got savings, and he's right. But I don't want to be the one who's carried.

say: I'd tell the senior partner **politely** to go slowly and keep people who know clients.
I **wouldn't make a fuss** in public.
think: The card's tasks are **my job**, line by line.
The firm would keep someone who **uses AI**, and that isn't me.
do: **Wait and see** what the firm actually brings in first.
Go on the **system training**, however reluctantly.
feel: **Anxious**, and cross with herself for not wanting to learn.
Uncomfortable at the idea of being **carried** by her partner.
S1.quote: After five years I can find any deed in the strongroom in ten seconds, and the software makes me feel like a beginner again.
fieldNote: Carla clearly sees her **task list** on the card and expects to be the one let go.
Her resistance is about **losing mastery**, not fear of computers.
Her partner's **secure trade** comforts her but hurts her pride.

steps.text: Wait to see which system the firm buys before acting
Attend the firm's case system training when it comes
Double the monthly transfer into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and someone should slow it down, though I don't know who. I'd probably just say that to friends over dinner. I'm not one for marches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd lose my job inside a year. All the thinking parts of my job go in 2028, and all that's left is lifting boxes of deeds, which a robot does three years later. It's not a nice thing to say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back hard, no Portugal, no new car, and keep everything we've saved. I'd look for anything hands-on, maybe working with Tom on his jobs, doing his paperwork and fetching parts. I'd also ask Mr Whitlock straight out how long I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. I'm someone who likes things to stay the same, and this is everything changing at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Working with Tom. Is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the only real plan I've got. Tom's been saying for years he needs someone to do his invoices and order parts. If I end up doing my boyfriend's invoices from the kitchen table, at least my boyfriend won't replace me with a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots come three years later. Does that affect Tom too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and that's what scares me. Tom has three more years than me, maybe. After that I don't know what either of us does.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and someone should slow it down.
I'd only say it to **friends over dinner**, not on a march.
think: I'd lose my job **inside a year**, once the thinking parts go.
What's left is **lifting boxes**, which robots do three years later.
do: Cut back hard: **no holiday**, no new car.
Start doing her partner's **invoices and parts** ordering.
Ask the senior partner **how long** she has.
feel: **Frightened**, as someone who likes things to stay the same.
S2.quote: If I end up doing my boyfriend's invoices from the kitchen table, at least my boyfriend won't replace me with a computer.
fieldNote: Carla expects to **lose her job** within a year and says it plainly.
Her fallback is her partner's **electrician business**, also exposed later.
Her centre outlook shows: she wants it slowed but **blames no one** in particular.

steps.text: Cancel the Portugal trip and the new car
Take over Tom's invoices and parts ordering for his electrical work
Ask Mr Whitlock directly how long her job will last

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to be sensible, and firms should train their staff rather than just sack them. I'd say that at work. Online, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years helps, but I'm not sure I'd use it well. I know myself. I'd keep thinking it might not happen until it's on my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm and keep saving, and I'd make myself do the training that comes along. In the second year I'd start doing Tom's paperwork in the evenings, so it's ready to become a proper job. And we'd hold off on starting a family until we see how it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but slower. Like a storm forecast for the weekend after next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hold off on a family. Is that something you'd planned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about it for around 2029. I don't want to be pregnant the same year a computer takes my job at the solicitors' office. So we'd wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned you might not use the time well. What would make you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing someone at work go. When Mr Whitlock lets the first person go, that's when I'd move. Before that I'd probably just keep filing.

say: I'd say firms should **train staff** rather than sack them.
I'd say it **at work**, but post nothing online.
think: Five years helps, but I might **not use it well**.
I'd likely wait until the change is **on my desk**.
do: Stay at the firm and **keep saving**.
Do her partner's **paperwork in the evenings** from year two.
Put off **starting a family** until things are clearer.
feel: **Worried**, but slower, like a storm forecast for later.
S3.quote: I don't want to be pregnant the same year a computer takes my job at the solicitors' office.
fieldNote: Carla is **honest** that she'd likely wait too long.
The trigger to act would be **seeing a colleague go**.
Five years affects her **family plans**, not just her job.

steps.text: Do Tom's electrical invoices in the evenings from year two
Keep saving the doubled monthly amount
Put off trying for a baby until the change is clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can change, so let's not panic. I'd say the same to my mum, who worries for me. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd tell myself I've got ages, and I'd probably believe it for a while. My job still goes in the end, though. I'd be 37 then, which isn't old, but it isn't 27 either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, have the family we planned, and keep saving. Maybe in year three or four I'd do a bookkeeping course, so I could properly run Tom's business side. I wouldn't do anything dramatic in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I could live with it. Ten years is long enough for me to pretend it isn't coming, and that's exactly the danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said that pretending is the danger. What would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom would, probably. He'd keep reminding me, gently. And having a child would make me plan, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Janice, the legal secretary, who's 54. She'd be 64 in 2036, so she might just about make it. I'd worry more about the younger ones like me who'd have to start over.

say: I'd say ten years is **a long time**, so let's not panic.
I'd keep it **practical**, even with her worried mum.
think: I'd tell myself **I've got ages** and believe it for a while.
My job still goes, and I'd be **37** by then.
do: **Carry on** working and have the family they planned.
Do a **bookkeeping course** in year three or four.
Avoid anything **dramatic** in the first year.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to live with it, aware she might pretend it isn't coming.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for me to pretend it isn't coming, and that's exactly the danger.
fieldNote: Carla admits ten years could let her **pretend** the change isn't coming.
Her partner and a **future child** are what would push her to plan.
She still expects her **desk job to end** by 2036.

steps.text: Keep working at Whitlock and Sons as normal
Start trying for a family as planned around 2029
Take a bookkeeping course in year three or four

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. There's no time for someone like me who takes three months to get used to a new system. What would help is firms having to keep staff on for a year while they retrain, so you're not just pushed out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be good at something old-fashioned. Being the person who knows where every deed is used to be a skill, and I'm scared it's turning into a habit nobody needs.

headlineQuote: Being the person who knows where every deed is used to be a skill, and I'm scared it's turning into a habit nobody needs.
portrait: Carla is a 27-year-old **solicitors' office administrator** who knows every file in the strongroom.
She **never uses AI** and finds each new system costs her months of stress.
Her **centre** outlook makes her want things slowed down without blaming anyone.
Her fallback in every bad picture is her **electrician partner's** business paperwork.
She admits she might **wait too long** to act, especially with ten years.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she needs months to adjust and there'd be no time.
whatWouldHelp: Firms **keeping staff on** for a year while they retrain.
